title: Mortgage Rates Hit 6.55%, Highest Since Iran War Began, as Housing Market Stalls
excerpt: The 30-year fixed mortgage rate climbed to levels not seen in 11 months as the US-Iran conflict drives oil prices and Treasury yields higher, crushing spring homebuying momentum.
body:
• The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 6.55% for the week ending July 16, its highest level since August 2025, according to Freddie Mac.
  • Pending home sales fell 5.4% month-over-month in June, according to the National Association of Realtors, as record-high home prices compound the affordability crisis.
  • June CPI inflation cooled to 3.5% from 4.2% in May, but renewed US-Iran fighting has pushed oil prices and Treasury yields higher, offsetting the positive inflation data.
  • Fannie Mae forecasts the 30-year rate will hold at 6.4% through year-end, but analysts say the path depends entirely on how the Iran conflict develops.

Rates Climb as Middle East Conflict Escalates

Mortgage rates surged to their highest level in nearly a year this week as the US-Iran conflict continued to roil energy markets and push bond yields higher, dealing another blow to prospective homebuyers who had hoped falling rates would revive the housing market.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage jumped to 6.55% for the week ending July 16, up 6 basis points from 6.49% the prior week and the highest since August 2025, according to data from Freddie Mac. The Wall Street Journal's Bankrate survey showed even higher readings, with the 30-year rate at 6.62% as of July 16.

"The highest mortgage rates in nearly a year and the record-high national median home price together are contributing to a tepid housing market that is especially difficult for first-time homebuyers."

— Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist, National Association of Realtors

Iran Conflict Drives the Market

The rate increase traced directly to renewed hostilities between the United States and Iran. In February, mortgage rates had briefly dipped below 6% for the first time in three and a half years, generating cautious optimism. But fighting that erupted in the Middle East days later sent rates climbing and never looked back.

A temporary ceasefire last month had offered a brief reprieve, with energy prices dropping and June inflation cooling to 3.5% from 4.2% in May, according to CPI data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Core inflation also eased to 2.6%.

But President Donald Trump's announcement on July 8 ending the ceasefire shattered those hopes. In an interview with Fox News, Trump threatened to target Iran's power plants and bridges unless Tehran returned to peace talks. Iran responded by threatening airstrikes throughout the region.

The escalation sent oil prices surging — gas prices jumped 15 cents in a week to $3.94 a gallon — and pushed Treasury yields higher, dragging mortgage rates up with them.

Housing Market Feels the Pain

The rate spike is throttling an already sluggish housing market. Pending home sales dropped 5.4% month-over-month in June and were 0.3% lower than a year ago, according to NAR data released Thursday. Mortgage applications fell 7% last week and were 2% below year-ago levels, per the Mortgage Bankers Association.

"Mortgage rates are essentially tied to the outcome of the Iran conflict at this point. If that situation festers later into the year or into 2027, I anticipate the 30-year fixed mortgage rate will be range bound in the 6-7% range."

— Corey Burr, Senior Vice President, TTR Sotheby's International Realty

Zillow senior economist Kara Ng noted that rates are "caught between cooler inflation data and renewed energy risks," adding that softer June inflation reduced the likelihood of a near-term Federal Reserve rate increase, but higher oil prices are keeping pressure on the inflation outlook.

What It Means for NRI Homebuyers

For Non-Resident Indians considering US property purchases, the rate environment presents a mixed picture. Rates remain well below the 7%-plus levels seen in early 2025, but the upward trajectory makes timing difficult.

Fannie Mae's July forecast projects the 30-year rate will hold at 6.4% through year-end before easing to 6.3% in early 2027 and 6.2% by late 2027. But the forecast's accuracy hinges on the Iran conflict, which was not factored into the July projections since they used June 30 data — before Trump ended the ceasefire.

Last week, bipartisan housing affordability legislation became law, aiming to boost supply through several measures including a first-of-its-kind limit on private equity purchases of single-family homes. However, the law does not address mortgage rates, which are set by the bond market.

Looking Ahead

Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones said her firm's midyear forecast still calls for rates to ease modestly in the second half, but conceded the near-term path remains "hostage" to the Iran situation. Until rates actually fall, she said, "buyers will keep feeling the pinch of stubbornly high borrowing costs even as other conditions improve."

The Federal Reserve has signaled it could raise the federal funds rate later this year if inflation remains elevated, a move that would push mortgage rates even higher. For now, the housing market's fate rests not with the Fed, but with events unfolding thousands of miles away in the Strait of Hormuz.
image_caption: A couple reviews mortgage paperwork at a home showing. Mortgage rates climbed to 6.55% this week, their highest level in 11 months, as the US-Iran conflict keeps bond yields elevated.
nri_angle: NRI homebuyers in the US face a difficult rate environment as the Iran conflict keeps mortgage costs elevated, though rates remain below 2025 peaks.
